    {
      "startEvent": 385,
      "endEvent": 389,
      "contextStartEvent": 368,
      "contextEndEvent": 406,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "any argument for moral skepticism is going to be based upon premises which are less obvious",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The endorsed quotation potentially discounts every skeptical argument before examining its premises (E385–389). No reason establishes that universal ranking. However, Craig supplies a perceptual analogy and explicitly allows defeaters (E371–383), so this may summarize a defeasible epistemic position rather than protect moral realism regardless of objections."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 493,
      "endEvent": 500,
      "contextStartEvent": 473,
      "contextEndEvent": 510,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "draw near to God and He will draw near to you",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["comfort"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The biblical promise supplies assurance that sincere seekers will experience God, without establishing its reliability or distinguishing divine experience from alternatives (E493–500). Craig expressly calls this nonargumentative (E473–478), yet offers it as a reason. Sincerity could shelter failures, but he never expressly declares unsuccessful seekers insincere; Millican later challenges this (E2938–2964)."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1355,
      "endEvent": 1359,
      "contextStartEvent": 1336,
      "contextEndEvent": 1365,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "prescriptions require prescribers and moral prescriptions require a moral prescriber",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "The repeatable formula supplies the bridge from moral obligation to a personal lawgiver. The surrounding questions and professional analogy do not establish why impersonal normative truths cannot obligate (E1350–1359). Earlier evolutionary reasoning addresses moral grounding generally (E351–367), but does not earn this specific necessity claim. No criticism-neutralizing device appears."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1720,
      "endEvent": 1743,
      "contextStartEvent": 1705,
      "contextEndEvent": 1745,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "he may well know that giving any more evidence of his existence would not lead more people to love",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["comfort"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Unseen divine knowledge supplies a possible explanation for withheld evidence; even obvious revelation might provoke resentment (E1720–1743). No evidence establishes these counterfactual reactions. However, Craig presents possibilities against Millican's probability claim, not an explicit rule insulating every evidential outcome. This is an ordinary defensive argument with uncertain protective reach."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2133,
      "endEvent": 2139,
      "contextStartEvent": 2125,
      "contextEndEvent": 2143,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "especially if God knew that for inviting more evidence wouldn't lead to a greater degree of salvation",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["comfort"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "After Millican's intervening rebuttal, Craig renews the appeal to God's possible knowledge that additional evidence would not improve salvation (E2133–2139). The needed counterfactual support remains absent. Its conditional form and earlier probability discussion (E1708–1743) leave uncertain whether it blocks contrary evidence categorically or merely challenges one expectation."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2240,
      "endEvent": 2250,
      "contextStartEvent": 2213,
      "contextEndEvent": 2253,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "the skepticism of biblical critics who deny the resurrection of Jesus is not predicated on historical grounds but philosophical grounds",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Craig categorically assigns critics' rejection to philosophical naturalism, excluding historical grounds, and links acceptance with open-mindedness (E2240–2250). Agreement about selected facts does not establish that diagnosis; Millican offered historical objections (E2056–2102). This protects the resurrection inference through a generalized account of dissent, although Craig also supplies historical argument rather than merely a slogan."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2863,
      "endEvent": 2876,
      "contextStartEvent": 2854,
      "contextEndEvent": 2909,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "it may well be that only in a world suffused with natural evil as well as moral evil",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["comfort"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Possible maximization of freely chosen salvation explains why God might permit natural evil (E2863–2876), without evidence connecting suffering to that optimum. Unrestricted purposes could absorb contrary patterns, but the claim is explicitly tentative. Craig also offers a separate, empirically answerable animal-pain argument (E2877–2909), so blanket protection is not established."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 1118,
      "endEvent": 1138,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "the absence of evidence is not necessarily evidence of absence",
      "explanation": "Craig qualifies the familiar phrase with an expectation-based criterion and contrasting examples: unobserved gold on Pluto versus a missing nearby planet. The surrounding reasoning earns the summary and explicitly identifies when absence does count against existence."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 674,
      "endEvent": 705,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "of course it's possible that the belief in God could be true even if we hold it for feeble reasons",
      "explanation": "Millican distinguishes a belief's truth from the reliability of its acquisition. He supports the latter criticism through conflicting religious conclusions and shared methods, expressly refusing the inference that dubious origins alone prove a belief false."
    }
  ]
